body.heading: Why the morning end matters more
paragraphs: People trying to fix their sleep usually attack the evening: earlier bedtimes, stricter routines. But bedtime is hard to command — you cannot make yourself sleepy by decree. Wake time, by contrast, is a decision. And a steady wake time quietly organises everything upstream of it.

Wake at the same time for a week or two and sleepiness starts arriving at a consistent hour in the evening, like a tide that has found its schedule. The body clock thrives on this regularity; it is, in a sense, what the clock is for.

body.heading: Most days is the honest target
paragraphs: Aim for a wake time you keep within about half an hour, most days — including, as much as life allows, weekends. The lie-in that feels like compensation can act like a small dose of jet lag, which is one reason Monday mornings feel the way they do.

“Most days” is doing real work in that sentence. Illness, travel, celebrations and small children all exist. A rhythm you return to after disruptions beats a perfect record you abandon at the first break.

body.heading: Make waking pleasant, not just punctual
paragraphs: Pair the alarm with the day’s first good thing: light, a drink you enjoy, music, a stretch, the dog’s enthusiasm. If waking is only ever a punishment, your half-asleep self will negotiate with the snooze button and win.

Protect the other end lightly too: once your wake time is steady, let your evening sleepiness choose the bedtime for a while. Many people are surprised to find the whole pattern settling from that single fixed point.

takeaway: Fix the wake time, keep it most days, and let sleepiness learn the schedule.
